salman-abuddarda.title: Salman and Abu al-Darda': “Give everyone their due”
salman-abuddarda.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ made Salman and Abu al-Darda' brothers. Salman visited Abu al-Darda' and saw Umm al-Darda' in shabby clothes. He asked: What is the matter with you? She said: Your brother Abu al-Darda' has no interest in this world. When night came, Abu al-Darda' went to pray and Salman said: Sleep. He went again and Salman said: Sleep. At the end of the night Salman said: Get up now — and they prayed. Salman told him: Your Lord has a right over you, your self has a right over you, and your family has a right over you, so give everyone their due. He went to the Prophet ﷺ and told him, and he said: “Salman spoke the truth.”
salman-abuddarda.historicalContext: In Madinah after the brotherhood established between the Emigrants and the Ansar.
salman-abuddarda.problemType: Being absorbed in one area (work, study, worship, a project) until oneself and one's family are neglected, or a neglectful, preoccupied spouse
salman-abuddarda.responseType: Rebalancing rights: Allah's right, the self's right and the family's right
principles: Every area of your life has a right that being busy with another does not cancel
Excess, even in good, may cause obligatory rights to be lost
Advice between friends should be practical and kind
A wife's right to attention is a religious right, not a luxury
modernApplications: Review your week: how many hours for work? family? sleep and rest? worship? Where is the imbalance?
If your spouse is too busy for you, ask a wise person they trust to advise them, as Salman did
Sleep and rest are the self's right, and giving them up is not heroism
Set clear limits on working time so it does not swallow home time
behaviorObservations: Salman noticed the wife's state and asked about her
He advised through action (sleep, get up now), not words alone
The Prophet ﷺ approved his advice: “Salman spoke the truth”
whatToAvoid: Justifying neglect of family with a “noble” preoccupation
Burdening yourself beyond capacity in the name of achievement
salman-abuddarda.reflection: Salman spoke the truth: give everyone their due; a good that wastes another right is not a complete good.
keywords: my husband doesn't care about me
i have no time for my family
i neglect my children because of work

quranRefs.relevance: Excess in one area at the expense of other rights goes against ease

hadithRefs.narrator: Abu Juhayfah (may Allah be pleased with him)

contrasts: The same rule the Prophet ﷺ gave the group who wanted to be extreme: “Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me”

hanzala.title: “Hanzalah has become a hypocrite!”: fluctuating faith is not hypocrisy
hanzala.eventDescription: Abu Bakr met Hanzalah and asked: How are you? He said: Hanzalah has become a hypocrite! When we are with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he reminds us of the Fire and Paradise, it is as if we can see them; but when we leave, we busy ourselves with our wives, children and affairs, and forget much. Abu Bakr said: By Allah, we experience the same. They went to the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “By the One in whose hand is my soul, if you remained as you are with me and in remembrance, the angels would shake your hands on your beds and in your streets. But, O Hanzalah, an hour and an hour” — three times.
hanzala.historicalContext: In Madinah; the hadith is in Sahih Muslim.
hanzala.problemType: Feeling like a hypocrite or weak in faith because one's spiritual state swings between devotion and heedlessness
hanzala.responseType: Understanding the fluctuating nature of the human heart, and continuing without self-punishment
principles: Faith fluctuating between strength and slackness is human nature
Your fear of hypocrisy is a sign of sincerity
Normal life (family, work, fun) is not the opposite of faith
What matters is that “the other hour” is not spent in sin
modernApplications: If you feel your faith in Ramadan or after a moving talk is higher than on other days, that is normal; do not judge yourself a hypocrite
Keep a steady minimum of worship on slack days
Confide what you feel to someone you trust, as Hanzalah did with Abu Bakr
Spend “the other hour” in what is permitted, not in what is forbidden
notToApplyTo: “An hour and an hour” does not mean an hour for obedience and an hour for sin, but an hour for remembrance and an hour for the permitted
behaviorObservations: The Prophet ﷺ reassured Hanzalah and did not rebuke him
He explained human nature realistically
He repeated “an hour and an hour” three times for emphasis
whatToAvoid: Punishing yourself for natural slackness
Abandoning worship on the grounds that “I'm a hypocrite anyway”
hanzala.reflection: If your devotion never wavered, the angels would shake your hand; but you are human, and yours is an hour and an hour.
keywords: my faith goes up and down
i no longer feel the sweetness of faith

quranRefs.relevance: The heart fluctuates, so ask Allah for steadfastness

hadithRefs.narrator: Hanzalah al-Usaydi (may Allah be pleased with him)

abudhar-jahiliyya.title: “You are a man with some ignorance in you”: when you are the one who offended
subCategories: Treatment of workers and domestic help
participants: A man Abu Dharr taunted about his mother
abudhar-jahiliyya.eventDescription: Abu Dharr exchanged insults with a man and taunted him about his mother, who was not Arab. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: “O Abu Dharr, did you taunt him about his mother? You are a man who still has some of the ignorance of pre-Islam in you. Your servants are your brothers whom Allah has placed under your authority. So whoever has his brother under his authority, let him feed him from what he eats and clothe him from what he wears, and do not burden them beyond their ability; and if you do, then help them.” After that, Abu Dharr was seen wearing a cloak and his servant wearing one just like it.
abudhar-jahiliyya.historicalContext: Narrated by Abu Dharr himself, admitting his mistake; he was among the earliest to embrace Islam.
abudhar-jahiliyya.problemType: Being the one in the wrong: taunting someone about their origin, colour or job, or mistreating those under your authority
abudhar-jahiliyya.responseType: Accepting frank criticism and radically changing one's behaviour in practice
principles: Even the righteous may fall into remnants of pre-Islamic ignorance
Those under your authority are your brothers, not your tools
Sincere advice may be frank, and accepting it is a sign of greatness
Real change shows in behaviour, not only in a verbal apology
modernApplications: If you hurt someone because of their origin, accent, colour or job, apologise to them openly
Review how you treat those who work for you: pay, rest, words, tasks
If someone points out a mistake frankly, accept before you defend
Make your change visible in action, as Abu Dharr and his servant wore the same cloak
behaviorObservations: The Prophet ﷺ confronted Abu Dharr frankly despite his standing
He tied the guidance to specific practical rules
Abu Dharr narrated the story himself, admitting his mistake
whatToAvoid: Justifying taunts as “just a joke”
Defending yourself before understanding the criticism
abudhar-jahiliyya.reflection: The greatest thing in the story is that Abu Dharr himself narrated it; whoever admits their ignorance begins to be freed from it.
keywords: i taunted him about his origin

quranRefs.relevance: No superiority by lineage or race

hadithRefs.narrator: Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (may Allah be pleased with him)

contrasts: The general rule announced to the nation: no Arab is superior to a non-Arab except by piety

mughith-barira.title: Mughith and Barirah: “I am only interceding”
mughith-barira.eventDescription: Barirah was a slave woman married to Mughith. When she was freed she was given the choice, and she chose to leave her husband. Mughith used to follow her through the streets of Madinah weeping, his tears running down his beard. The Prophet ﷺ said to al-‘Abbas: “O ‘Abbas, are you not amazed at how much Mughith loves Barirah and how much Barirah dislikes Mughith?” The Prophet ﷺ said to her: “Why not go back to him?” She said: O Messenger of Allah, are you commanding me? He said: “I am only interceding.” She said: I have no need of him.
mughith-barira.historicalContext: In Madinah. The story is a basis for a woman's freedom to choose whether to remain with her husband after being freed.
prophetTraits: Mercy to the one in love
mughith-barira.problemType: One-sided love, a relationship/engagement/marriage ended by the other person's wish, or the pain of emotional rejection
mughith-barira.responseType: Acknowledging the pain without contempt, courteous intercession, then respecting the other person's decision
principles: Feelings of love are not a fault; the Prophet ﷺ sympathised with Mughith and did not mock him
Hearts cannot be forced, and everyone has the right to their emotional decision
Courteous intercession is legitimate; insistence and coercion are not
Accepting “no” is part of maturity
modernApplications: If you were rejected or your relationship ended, allow yourself to grieve without despising yourself
You may ask once courteously or have someone mediate, but if the answer is no, respect it and do not pursue
Do not use family or religious pressure to force someone to stay with you
Direct your energy towards healing: company, work, worship, time
notToApplyTo: Love does not justify a forbidden relationship; chastity remains required even in intense attachment
behaviorObservations: The Prophet ﷺ noticed Mughith's sorrow and marvelled at it with compassion
He interceded for him gently without commanding
He respected Barirah's decision when she said no
whatToAvoid: Despising the one in love or mocking their pain
Forcing the other person into a relationship they do not want
mughith-barira.reflection: Even the intercession of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not force a heart; love is asked for, not imposed, and refusal is respected, not pursued.
keywords: i love her and she doesn't love me

quranRefs.relevance: Separation should be with kindness and without coercion

hadithRefs.narrator: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them)

fatima-khadim.title: Fatimah asks for a servant: the strength of tasbih in exhaustion
fatima-khadim.eventDescription: Fatimah complained of what her hands suffered from the hand mill. She came to the Prophet ﷺ to ask for a servant but did not find him, so she told ‘A'ishah. The Prophet ﷺ came to them after they had gone to bed, sat between them and said: “Shall I not teach you something better than what you asked me for? When you go to bed, say Allahu akbar thirty-four times, Subhan Allah thirty-three times and Alhamdu lillah thirty-three times. That is better for you than a servant.”
fatima-khadim.historicalContext: In Madinah, in the humble, simple home of ‘Ali and Fatimah.
fatima-khadim.problemType: Exhaustion from housework, childcare or accumulating daily responsibilities
fatima-khadim.responseType: Asking for legitimate help, while building daily spiritual strength through remembrance
principles: Complaining of tiredness and asking for help are not faults
Remembrance gives real strength that helps with burdens
The Prophet ﷺ came himself to his daughter's home and sat between her and her husband with tenderness
Not everything we ask for is granted, but the alternative may be more beneficial
modernApplications: If you are exhausted by housework, do not be shy about asking your husband or family for help
Make tasbih before sleep a daily habit (33 Subhan Allah, 33 Alhamdu lillah, 34 Allahu akbar)
A husband should share household burdens, as the Prophet ﷺ served his family
Lower the standards of perfection at home; rest comes before perfection
notToApplyTo: This does not mean refusing domestic help for those who can afford it
behaviorObservations: The Prophet ﷺ went to his daughter himself
He sat between them with humility and tenderness
He offered a practical spiritual alternative
whatToAvoid: Leaving all the household burdens on the wife alone
Neglecting the spiritual side under the pressure of tasks
fatima-khadim.reflection: She asked for a servant to help her hands, and was given remembrance to help her heart; when the heart is strong, the hand grows strong.
keywords: the children have worn me out
no one helps me at home

quranRefs.relevance: Remembrance gives the soul strength that helps the body

hadithRefs.narrator: ‘Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him)

iqilha-tawakkul.title: “Tie it and trust”: balancing the means and trust in Allah
iqilha-tawakkul.eventDescription: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah, should I tie her and trust in Allah, or leave her untied and trust in Allah? (meaning his camel). He said: “Tie her and trust in Allah.”
iqilha-tawakkul.historicalContext: A simple question from an ordinary man, whose answer became a major principle in understanding trust in Allah.
iqilha-tawakkul.problemType: Being torn between excessive worry and over-planning on one side, and passive reliance on the other
iqilha-tawakkul.responseType: Taking all the means, then leaving the result to Allah with a peaceful heart
principles: Trust is the work of the heart and the means are the work of the limbs; neither replaces the other
Once the means are taken, let worry go, for it adds nothing
The birds “go out in the morning”: trust includes going out and striving
Excessive worry after taking the means is a shortfall in trust
modernApplications: Write a list of the means available to you for your problem (study, treatment, job search) and carry them out
After doing your part, say: I put my trust in Allah — and leave the circular thinking about the result
If you keep worrying, ask: is there any means I have not taken? If not, this is the time for trust
Do not be passive on the grounds that “provision is written”: the birds go out every morning
behaviorObservations: He answered with a few words that contain the whole method
He did not rebuke the questioner for his simple question
whatToAvoid: Passive reliance that abandons the means
Excessive worry after the means are taken
iqilha-tawakkul.reflection: Tie your camel with your hand, and release your heart to Allah; the rope is for the camel, not the heart.
keywords: i think too much about the future
i don't know what will happen

hadithRefs.narrator: Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him)
‘Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him)

hatab-karama.title: A bundle of firewood: the dignity of work, however humble
hatab-karama.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ said: “That one of you takes his rope and brings a bundle of firewood on his back and sells it, and Allah thereby saves his face, is better for him than asking people, whether they give him or refuse him.” The prophets themselves worked with their hands: Dawud (peace be upon him) ate from the work of his own hands.
hatab-karama.historicalContext: One of the Prophet's ﷺ repeated instructions in Madinah to build a productive society.
hatab-karama.problemType: Embarrassment at accepting work below one's level or qualifications, or depending on others financially
hatab-karama.responseType: Accepting available lawful work with dignity, while striving for better
principles: Lawful work, however humble, is more honourable than begging
Dignity lies in financial independence
The prophets worked with their hands
A small beginning is not the end of the road
modernApplications: Do not wait too long for the ideal job; start with available lawful work, even temporarily
Ignore society's view of humble jobs; your measure is the religion's measure
Keep developing your skills while you work
If you depend on your family while able to work, take a step towards independence
notToApplyTo: This does not condemn those forced to seek help because of real inability
behaviorObservations: He encouraged any lawful work
He gave a tangible image (rope and firewood)
He linked work with preserving dignity
whatToAvoid: Looking down on humble work
Relying on others while able
hatab-karama.reflection: A bundle of firewood on your back is better than an outstretched hand; dignity is measured not by the kind of work but by its cleanness.
keywords: i'm ashamed of a humble job
a job that doesn't match my degree
i don't want a simple job

quranRefs.relevance: Seeking provision through work is worship

hadithRefs.narrator: al-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam (may Allah be pleased with him)
al-Miqdam ibn Ma‘dikarib (may Allah be pleased with him)

jar-mataa.title: The man who complained of his neighbour: a smart, practical solution to harm
participants: A man complaining of his neighbour
jar-mataa.eventDescription: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ complaining about his neighbour. He said: “Go and be patient.” He came two or three times, and the Prophet ﷺ said: “Go and put your belongings out in the street.” He put his belongings in the street, and people began asking him, and he told them his story, and people began cursing the harmful neighbour: may Allah do such and such to him. His neighbour came to him and said: Go back in; you will see nothing from me that you dislike.
jar-mataa.historicalContext: In Madinah; the hadith is in Abu Dawud with a good chain.
jar-mataa.problemType: Repeated harm from a neighbour or someone close, where patience has not worked
jar-mataa.responseType: A gradual approach: patience first, then a practical solution using legitimate public opinion without aggression
principles: Patience is the first step, not the only one
The wronged may make their grievance known by legitimate means
A smart solution can make confrontation unnecessary
Legitimate social pressure may deter the one causing harm
modernApplications: Start with patience and direct dialogue with the harmful neighbour
If the harm continues, involve a third party: neighbours, building management, community elders
Document repeated harm, and use official channels if needed
Look for a creative solution that embarrasses the one causing harm without attacking them
notToApplyTo: This does not permit defaming with lies or attacking
In cases of danger, go directly to the official authorities
behaviorObservations: He commanded patience first
When the complaint was repeated he changed the approach
He chose a solution in which the wronged did not attack anyone
whatToAvoid: Attacking the harmful neighbour
Endless patience with harm that could be removed
jar-mataa.reflection: Patience is a first step, but wisdom may open a door that patience alone did not.
keywords: i've been patient with my neighbour

quranRefs.relevance: Kindness to the neighbour is obligatory, and harming him is a major sin

hadithRefs.narrator: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)

contrasts: Here: dealing with a harmful neighbour; there: the general foundation of the neighbour's great right

saad-wasiyya.title: Sa‘d in his illness: “Better that you leave your heirs well off”
saad-wasiyya.eventDescription: Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas fell so ill during the Farewell Pilgrimage that he was close to death. The Prophet ﷺ visited him, and Sa‘d said: I have wealth and only a daughter to inherit from me. Shall I give two thirds of my wealth in charity? He said: No. — Half? — No. — A third? He said: “A third, and a third is a lot. It is better that you leave your heirs well off than leave them dependent, begging from people. You will not spend anything seeking Allah's countenance except that you will be rewarded for it, even what you put in your wife's mouth.” Sa‘d recovered and lived many years after that.
saad-wasiyya.historicalContext: In Makkah during the Farewell Pilgrimage, in the tenth year after the migration.
saad-wasiyya.problemType: Fear of death or illness, and thinking about the family's financial future and one's will
saad-wasiyya.responseType: Moderation in spending, securing the family, and remembering that spending on family is worship
principles: Securing the family's future is good, not stinginess
Spending on family is charity with the right intention
Moderation even in good works
Serious illness does not necessarily mean the end; Sa‘d lived long afterwards
modernApplications: Plan financially for your family (savings, lawful insurance, an Islamic will) without considering it a lack of trust in Allah
Keep the intention in everything you spend on your home; it is worship
Consult a qualified scholar about wills and inheritance
Do not let fear of illness push you into hasty financial decisions
notToApplyTo: Details of wills and inheritance should be referred to a qualified scholar
behaviorObservations: The Prophet ﷺ visited Sa‘d in his illness
He brought him down step by step to a third
He widened the meaning of reward to include a morsel for one's wife
whatToAvoid: Neglecting the heirs' rights in the name of charity
Considering saving for one's family contrary to trust in Allah
saad-wasiyya.reflection: Even the morsel you place in your wife's mouth is charity; your home is a place of worship if your intention is right.
keywords: i'm sick and worried about my children
what will i leave my children
worried about my family after me

hadithRefs.narrator: Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him)

qabil-habil.title: The two sons of Adam: “Allah only accepts from the righteous”
subCategories: Self-restraint in the face of aggression
qabil-habil.eventDescription: The two sons of Adam each offered a sacrifice; it was accepted from one and not from the other. Instead of the one whose offering was not accepted examining himself, he turned his anger on his brother and said: “I will surely kill you.” His brother answered calmly: “Indeed, Allah only accepts from the righteous,” and then said: “If you should raise your hand against me to kill me, I shall not raise my hand against you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.” His soul made it easy for him to kill his brother, so he killed him and became one of the losers — then one of the regretful, when he did not even know how to hide his brother's body.
qabil-habil.historicalContext: The first crime in human history as the Quran tells it in Surah al-Ma'idah, driven by envy that the other's deed had been accepted.
qabil-habil.problemType: Envy of a brother's, colleague's or relative's success, or being envied and treated with hostility because of your success
qabil-habil.responseType: Treating envy by reforming oneself and one's work, and not answering aggression in kind
emotionsAddressed: Feeling wronged by the other being preferred
principles: Acceptance by Allah is tied to piety, so the way to it is reforming yourself, not tearing others down
Envy progresses: feeling, then words, then action — so cut it off at the start
You are not obliged to answer aggression in kind; fear of Allah is strength, not weakness
Regret after it is too late does not bring back what was lost
modernApplications: If your brother or colleague excels, ask: what did he do, and what can I improve in my work? — instead of: why him?
If you notice yourself wishing someone would lose a blessing, pray secretly for blessing for them; it is the strongest cure for envy
If you are envied, do not show off in front of the envier or enter into hostility with them; protect yourself with remembrance and boundaries
When you feel angry at someone's success, delay any reaction until you calm down
notToApplyTo: Not raising one's hand does not mean giving up legitimate self-defence in real danger; protection and turning to the relevant authorities are obligatory
behaviorObservations: The wronged brother answered calmly and returned the matter to its true measure: piety
He reminded his brother of the fear of Allah before the act happened
The envier did not reform himself but moved to eliminate the one who succeeded
whatToAvoid: Interpreting someone else's success as injustice to you
Feeding envy with constant comparison and watching
qabil-habil.reflection: Before asking “Why did Allah accept from him?”, ask “What is missing from my work for it to be accepted?”

quranRefs.relevance: The envier sees the problem in his brother, and the Quran returns it to him: improve your work, do not tear down others

quranRefs.context: Where envy ends when left untreated
